detailed_rationale:
Hindustan Construction Company (HCC) is a legacy EPC/infrastructure contractor whose investment case for several years has centred on monetising a large book of arbitration awards from historical project disputes, alongside shrinking core construction operations. FY26 standalone net profit rose a striking 142% YoY to Rs 205.8cr - but this needs to be read against the source of that cash: HCC raised Rs 1,000cr via a Rights Issue (December 2025) and recovered arbitration proceeds via bank guarantees of Rs 720cr in FY26, using 'capital infusion, arbitration realisations and internal accruals' (per the company's own debt-reduction commentary) to cut debt 38% YoY to Rs 1,995cr from Rs 3,197cr. HCC also transferred arbitration awards worth Rs 1,979cr to a wholly-owned subsidiary (HCC Contract Solutions Limited) as part of restructuring how those claims are monetised. None of this is core-business operating performance - it is balance-sheet repair funded by equity dilution and legacy-litigation cash realisation.

Meanwhile the actual construction business kept shrinking: Q4 FY26 standalone revenue of Rs 988.7cr was down roughly 26-27% YoY (from ~Rs 1,330cr a year earlier), continuing a multi-year contraction that shows up in the quant data as a -21.7% 3-year revenue CAGR and -29.2% 1-year revenue decline - both among the steepest in this batch. EBITDA margins compressed in the same period per multiple trackers, and profit was sequentially lower quarter-on-quarter within FY26 itself (Rs 44.6cr in Q4 vs Rs 85.9cr in Q3), suggesting the FY26 profit headline was front-loaded by one-off items rather than building momentum through the year. Quality score in our data (60.9) looks respectable, likely reflecting the ROCE (29.3%) and improved leverage optics post-rights-issue/debt paydown, but interest coverage remains thin at 1.2x and the balance-sheet flag is RED - both consistent with a company still working through legacy financial stress even after the recent repair steps.
recommendation_rationale: The headline net-profit growth is a textbook earnings-quality flag rather than a reason to rescue this to Hold: it is substantially explained by a Rs 1,000cr equity raise and one-off arbitration-award monetisation, not by the core EPC business, which actually shrank ~26-29% this year on top of a -21.7% 3-year CAGR. With interest coverage still thin (1.2x) and a RED balance-sheet flag persisting even after the debt paydown, we see no basis to override the quant Sell - if anything, stripping out the one-off arbitration/rights-issue effects makes the underlying picture look weaker than the reported PAT growth suggests.
summary: HCC's reported profit jumped sharply this year, but that improvement was driven mainly by a large equity raise and one-off recoveries from legacy arbitration claims, not by its core construction business, which continued to shrink at a steep pace. With thin interest cover and a red balance-sheet flag still in place, we recommend Sell.
positive_para: HCC has made genuine progress cleaning up its balance sheet - debt down 38% YoY to Rs 1,995cr, aided by a Rs 1,000cr rights issue and Rs 720cr of arbitration-related cash recoveries - which reduces near-term insolvency-style risk versus where the company stood a few years ago, and ROCE on the reported numbers (29.3%) looks strong.
negative_para: The core construction business is contracting sharply, not growing: revenue fell roughly 26-29% year-on-year in the most recent quarter and by a similar magnitude over the past year, continuing a multi-year decline (3-year revenue CAGR -21.7%). Most of this year's profit improvement traces back to one-off arbitration-claim monetisation and equity dilution rather than operating performance, and profit was already declining sequentially within FY26 (Q4 down from Q3). Interest coverage remains thin (1.2x) and the balance-sheet flag is RED despite the recent debt paydown - the legacy financial stress has not fully cleared.
reverse_dcf_judgment: A ~36x trailing PE on a business whose core revenue is shrinking by a quarter or more per year, and whose reported profit is substantially one-off-driven (arbitration monetisation, rights-issue-funded deleveraging) rather than operating-earnings growth, cannot be justified by ordinary business fundamentals. Strip out the one-offs and the earnings base supporting that multiple looks considerably smaller. Judgment: rich relative to demonstrated, repeatable operating earnings.
